claims.text: A rapid, transient temperature impulse can reduce all metal precursors nearly synchronously.
Synchronous precursor reduction causes simultaneous nucleation of the constituent metals.
Simultaneous nucleation locks in a uniform elemental distribution.
Significant atomic diffusion can induce phase separation in these nanoparticles.
Near-simultaneous formation of early-stage nuclei prevents elemental segregation and phase separation.
Near-simultaneous nucleation preserves homogeneous interparticle interfaces.
A rapid temperature impulse minimizes the time available for disparate precursor-reduction kinetics.
A rapid temperature impulse minimizes the time available for atomic interdiffusion.
Concurrent nucleation establishes a uniform alloy structure that resists later phase separation.
Rapid thermal-pulse processing will produce nanoparticles with homogeneous phase formation and evenly distributed elements.
Rapid thermal-pulse processing will produce nanoparticles with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio.
Conventional slow heating will lead to phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
Slow heating permits differential reduction and atomic diffusion that often cause phase inhomogeneity or segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies when differences among constituent-metal reduction kinetics are small enough to be overcome by rapid heating.
The mechanism may fail for metals with extremely disparate reduction potentials.
The mechanism may fail when the thermal pulse cannot be applied uniformly to all precursor sites.
Rapid thermal treatment should improve catalytic properties relative to conventional slow heating.
